description: We are CrewSync,Our project SYMBIOSIS X, aims to advance astronaut health monitoring through AI-powered anomaly detection, predictive analytics, and autonomous decision support for deep-space missions. We combine interests in AI, machine learning, software engineering, data science, and healthcare. We value innovation, collaboration, and real-world impact, and welcome expertise in space medicine and UI/UX design.
summary:
SYMBIOSIS X lets an astronaut check their own health during a mission. We built it inside a small
playable mission so we could test it under pressure instead of on an empty form.
The astronaut enters a reading, for example resting heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, temperature,
sleep, mood or symptoms. We compare it with two things and keep them separate: the astronaut's own
normal values, and a published range for people on Earth. The result says why it was flagged. If we
don't know how a reading was taken, we say "unknown" rather than "normal".
Readings taken the same way build a trend. When a reading falls outside the astronaut's own range, the
next step becomes "measure again and talk to the crew medical officer". Chest-pain and collapse drills
are handled by the crew on board, without waiting for Earth. NASA's Human Research Program names
distance from Earth as one of the five main hazards of spaceflight, and that is the problem we designed
around. Flight surgeons on Earth get a short case status after a simulated 300-second delay. The
readings and private notes stay with the crew.
details:
There are two parts that share one mission clock. The health tool is where an astronaut measures and reviews their health. Flight is the game: four fictional astronauts launch on the ship Horizon, dock with the ISS and come back to Earth. Along the way the CO2 scrubber fails, a wristband gives a bad reading, two crew go on a spacewalk and Mara runs a chest-pain drill. Working features Seven health readings, each with its unit (bpm, mmHg, mg/dL, °C, minutes, mood from 1 to 5, a list of symptoms) and a short note on how to measure it and which device to use. Two checks on every reading: one against the astronaut's personal baseline, one against an Earth range from MedlinePlus, the American Heart Association or the American Diabetes Association. The Earth range is only used when the measuring method matches, so lab glucose limits are not applied to a finger-stick meter. Each result names the rule and source it used. Trends from comparable readings only. Three resting heart rates at least 20 bpm above baseline open a review, and the review lists the readings that caused it. A reminder schedule for each reading. An out-of-range result moves the reminder to "repeat and review with the crew medical officer". Chest-pain and collapse drills that work during a communication blackout. The case names who responds on board and lists short training steps. An open emergency comes before routine reminders. A Ground view that arrives 300 mission seconds late and shows only a case ID, priority and status, plus when it was observed, when it arrived and how old it is. Heart rate, wearable data, check-in notes and medical history are never sent. A ship twin: cabin CO2 goes up when the scrubber fails and down after the repair, and the astronaut who was exposed gets flagged. A body figure for each astronaut with anatomy, skeleton, muscle, heart and lung, sensor and suit layers. Clicking it shows which sensor took which reading and how old the sample is. A check on wearable data. A wristband sample spoiled by movement is held back, a crewmate takes the reading again, and the new one is accepted.

How it works A Python and FastAPI service runs the mission clock and the health rules, and stores everything in SQLite. Each run can be read in two ways. The crew view has the full private record. The Ground view is built from a fixed list of fields that are allowed to leave the ship. The React app and the Flight game both read from these views. Runs use a fixed seed (4242), so a mission plays out the same way each time. How we tested it We generated a 30-day made-up mission with 960 scheduled readings and hid problems in it: abnormal values, slow drifts, sensor errors, late and duplicate packets, missed readings and emergencies. The tool caught all 78 of the hidden events. On 20 clean crew-days it raised no false review, and it never showed a missing reading as normal. Our automated tests also pass from a clean checkout: 120 backend unit tests, 74 integration tests, 56 browser tests, and one privacy test that checks nothing private reaches Ground. Who it helps The astronaut gets a quick check with a reason they can read. The crew member who responds to an emergency gets a case they can act on without waiting for Earth. Flight surgeons get data that tells them how old it is, without private details they don't need. Limitations All astronauts and readings are fictional. We did not use any real health records. The personal ranges, the review rule, the 3,200 ppm CO2 limit and the 300-second delay are our demo choices. They are not clinical limits or NASA limits. The emergency steps are training placeholders based on American Red Cross first-aid pages. They are not approved medical procedures. The tool says when to measure again and when to bring in the crew medical officer or Ground. It does not suggest treatment. The 30-second demo and parts of the Flight game are scripted playback. The health tool itself runs live through the API. Future plans Connect real devices: a wrist sensor, a blood pressure cuff and a glucose meter. Add NASA's general countermeasure advice from the HRP risk pages, such as exercise, sleep timing and lighting. Ask flight surgeons to review our review rules and emergency steps. Tools and languages Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLite and pytest. Frontend: JavaScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS and HTML canvas. Browser tests: Playwright. We did not use hardware; the sensors are simulated.
dataRefs: 15 rows of absorbed dose rate in μGy/hour from 1 April 2022, shown as radiation background on the crew health page. This is instrument data, not anyone's personal dose. We traced one row from the export file to the screen and recorded the file hashes.
Sample types, assays, time points and units, shown on the medical research card.
The heart, sleep, behavioural health and immune risks helped us choose which readings to track.
Why emergencies are handled on board and why Ground data arrives late. NASA analog missions practise delays of up to five minutes each way; our 300-second delay is within that.
Repeated measurements against a personal baseline, sleep and mood self-reports, and a crew medical officer on board during communication delays (Tempus Pro).
Decision support on board when Earth is far away.
Cited so nobody mistakes our demo CO2 limit for the NASA requirement.

projectRefs: Background for the radiation panel: the station uses dedicated radiation instruments, and neutrons make up about 30% of ISS radiation. The chart itself uses NASA RadLab data, not CSA data.
Crews going further out will rely less on Earth for emergency medical help. That is why our emergencies are handled on board.
Inspiration4 cabin CO2 and heart rate variability, shown as research background. We don't claim one causes the other.
